title: Specificity: swap generic words for concrete ones to write clearer, funnier copy
summary: Jason Cohen argues the single best writing advice for marketing copy, pitches and humor is to be specific. He walks through a workshop that replaces generic words, tightens accuracy, adds named examples, and shows how specificity is the easiest route to funny.

principles.text: The best advice for any writing (marketing, blog, sales pitch, investor pitch, humor) is to be specific.
principles.quote: My single best advice about writing--whether for marketing copy, blogging, a sales pitch, an investor pitch, or even humor, is: BE SPECIFIC

principles.text: Generic words signal lazy writing and get interpreted differently by each reader, so the message received is unclear.
principles.quote: Generic words are a sure sign of lazy writing.

principles.text: Move from merely true to accurate: pick the precise word (e.g. "evangelist" not "expert") that says what you actually mean.
principles.quote: After disposing with the obviously-useless generic words we're still left with words which, while technically correct, are still not contributing enough to the meaning and persuasiveness of your writing.

principles.text: Concrete examples make persuasive arguments clearer, more believable, harder to counter, and easier to apply and research.
Naming real people and industries makes a claim tangible, even if the reader has never heard of them.
principles.quote: See how much more evocative it is to put a name to the evangelists; even if you've never heard of those guys, knowing their names makes it tangible.

principles.text: Specific nouns, verbs and adjectives are the easiest way to be funny; exaggerate, invent an example, or highlight the absurd.
principles.quote: It's odd but true that almost any statement can be made funny merely by being specific, and there are many ways to do it.
